title: A great character
hook: and you are of a great character (68:4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Qalam, the pen and all that people write. Your line was even your grocery list counts. Three verses on, the surah turns from the pen to a person.

Mecca, the early years. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is being called crazy by people he grew up with, in public, in the market. Some laugh, some threaten. That's the setting of surah al-Qalam: a man mocked by his own town. Verse two answers the insult: by the grace of your Lord, you are not mad. Then verse four says something nobody in that market would have predicted. It doesn't defend his sanity. It praises his character.

Verse four, in Pickthall's translation: "And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature." Nature is Pickthall's word. The Arabic is khuluq, and most people today translate it character: the moral shape of a person, how they treat others, what they do when nobody's grading them. And the verse says 'azim: great, immense, tremendous. Khuluq comes from the root kh-l-q, the same root as khalq, creation. Your khalq is how you were made: face, height, voice. Your khuluq is how you've been shaped, the character you carry. One is given; the other, Muslims say, is worked on all your life. Years later someone asked 'A'ishah, the Prophet's wife, what his character was like. Her answer, in Sahih Muslim, is famous: his character was the Qur'an. If you want to see what the book looks like walking around, look at how he lived. Patient with the people who mocked him. Gentle with children. Mending his own clothes. Another hadith, in the Muwatta of Imam Malik, reports him saying he was sent to perfect good character. And a hadith in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi says nothing will weigh heavier on a believer's scale on the Day of Judgment than good character. It doesn't dismiss prayer or charity; it just says nothing outweighs character. So al-Qalam's answer to the insult isn't an argument. It's a description. You can call a man crazy. But look at how he treats you while you're doing it.

Choose one trait: patience, gentleness, honesty, generosity, keeping a promise. Think of the next place it'll be tested, a meeting, a commute, a kid who won't put on shoes, and picture it showing up there in one specific action: a softer word, a pause, the truth told plainly. Rehearse it once in your mind, start to finish.
Khuluq. Character, the moral shape a person is formed into. In 68:4 the Prophet is praised for a great one: khuluqin 'azim. Today's word.
Your line: great character. Nothing weighs more on the scale than that. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims treat good character (husn al-khuluq) as central to the faith, and look to the Prophet's conduct, described by 'A'ishah as 'the Qur'an', as its model; many books of hadith have whole chapters on manners and character.

chat.says: When people called the Prophet crazy, what did the Qur'an praise him for?
options: His great character, khuluq: how he treated people, even those mocking him.
His winning arguments, which proved to the town he wasn't mad.
His family name and rank, which earned him the town's respect.
chat.meaning: 68:4 answers the insult by praising his great character, and 'A'ishah said his character was the Qur'an.
